summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory under military administration by Morocco, and the territory stands under Morocco's penal code wherever its security services operate. Same-sex intimacy is criminalised, carrying six months to three years of imprisonment, and the broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and separately records homosexuality as illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades. A July 2017 global legality roundup lists it as a criminalising jurisdiction, and several rights indexes and advocacy groups record the same conduct as punishable by up to three years in prison for both males and females. Both claimed frameworks therefore record criminalisation, and a visitor cannot rely on either to displace the other.

Rights reviews document involuntary outing of trans people, discrepancies in expression at checkpoints and in registry records, an absence of gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition; a 2021 route to recognition covers intersex people only. Morocco's religious establishment has publicly condemned transition.

Enforcement stacks on top of the occupation. Morocco charged 170 people in a single year, an organised outing campaign ran in 2020, and rights defenders are prosecuted at the territory's own courts. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence, so the protection machinery a trans visitor would expect to reach is absent in practice as well as in statute.
tangentialFactors:
The region was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalized in Spain until 1979, which shaped the legal and social inheritance the territory carries into the present.

Most residents of the territory are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon, a social pressure that sits alongside the penal provisions rather than below them.

Same-sex activity is also illegal in Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims. The parent framework is therefore not a permissive backdrop against which the disputed claim can be read; the criminalising direction is the same on both sides of the sovereignty dispute.
localsOnly:
A 2009 United States Committee for Refugees and Immigration (USCRI) report found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape, indicating that the charge is applied by camp authorities as well as by Moroccan courts.

Human Rights Watch reported on 9 December 2005 the trial of seven Sahrawi human-rights defenders charged with fomenting illegal protests, calling the charges dubious and demanding a fair trial. The dispatch documents Moroccan state authority exercised over the territory through security services and courts, and detention of Sahrawi activists, which is the legal framework a resident stands under.

A 2018 legal study recorded LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: in 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it', while several other sources record a penalty of up to three years for the same conduct. No primary constitutional text is in the inventory, so which statement reflects the operative instrument is not settled here.

Unresolved: the inventory does not establish how far Morocco's penal code reaches across the whole territory or whether its application is confined to areas where security services operate; the sources state the framework generally rather than mapping its geographic limits.

Not sourced: no source in the inventory addresses border or visa screening of trans travellers, the specific penalty attached to visibly trans expression under Moroccan law, or any procedure by which a trans visitor could obtain legal gender recognition in the territory.
